fields.meta_description: Describe your review stages and get a content approval workflow that brings in experts by topic and chases late reviews.
fields.h1: Build a Content Approval Workflow That Routes Every Draft
fields.hero_description: Build a content approval workflow that sends each draft to the right reviewer and records who approved it and when.
fields.features_heading: What a Content Approval Workflow Handles
fields.features_subheading: Reviewers still judge the work. The app carries each piece to them, chases the slow ones, and keeps the record.
fields.feature_1:
Reviewers chosen by what the draft says

Routes every piece to its editor first, then adds a product expert when the copy cites a figure and legal when it names a price. Each rule is a sentence you wrote, not a setting.
fields.feature_2:
Decisions taken in Slack or email

Sends each reviewer the draft link with Approve and Request changes buttons. The click is written back to the content record with the reviewer's name, the version, and the time.
fields.feature_3:
Reminders before a publish date slips

Nudges any reviewer who has not answered within two working days, and alerts the content lead on day three. A publish date in the calendar moves only when a person moves it.
fields.feature_4:
Revision rounds counted per asset

Counts each round of changes on a post or a design file. Once an asset passes the limit set in its brief, the next round goes to a senior reviewer instead of back to the designer.
fields.feature_5:
An approval history you can search

Keeps every version, comment, and decision in a database you own. Filter it by campaign or by approver to see exactly which version was cleared for release, and who cleared it.
fields.feature_6:
The review app, yours as code

Exports the review app with its routing rules to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Adding a stage for a new content type, or a backup approver, takes one more prompt.

fields.usecase_heading: Where Content Teams Add Review Steps
fields.tab_content_1:
Any draft quoting a benchmark also goes to an expert

A writer moves the post to Ready in the content calendar, and the managing editor gets it in Slack. Drafts that cite a benchmark go to the product expert next. Once both approve, the post is scheduled in WordPress for Thursday at 10:00 AM, with both approvals saved on its row.
fields.tab_content_2:
Clients answer next week's posts from a single link

On Friday the agency sends Brightside Dental one review link with its 9 posts for next week. The practice manager approves 7 and leaves 2 unanswered. Comments on any post go back to the writer. When those 2 sit for two days, the account manager gets a reminder. No post is scheduled without a client decision.
fields.tab_content_3:
A third round of edits goes to the creative director

Six ad sizes for the spring campaign come back from the design lead after round 2. The brief includes 2 rounds of changes. When the marketing manager asks for round 3, the app sends that request to the creative director, who decides whether another pass is worth the time.
fields.tab_content_4:
No send until a principal approves the email

The market update email waits in the review queue until a registered principal at the wealth firm approves it. FINRA Rule 2210 requires that approval for retail communications. The app stores the principal's name with the approved version and the time, then releases the send. Any edit after approval reopens the review.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Content Approval Workflow
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to decide who reviews what, then build a content approval workflow that routes each draft and records each decision.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Name a reviewer for each stage
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with the content you publish most often. For each type, write down who drafts it, who reviews it today, and where it usually stalls. The slowest handoff on that list is where the new workflow earns its keep first.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Give every stage one named reviewer and a backup for when they are away. Keep fixed stages few: an editor and a brand owner cover most routine pieces. Each extra fixed stage is one more queue every draft has to wait in.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Describe in plain sentences when a piece needs more than the usual review. It quotes a statistic, names a price, mentions a customer, or touches a regulated product. Emergent turns those sentences into the rules that add a reviewer.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Connect the content calendar, Slack or email for decisions, and WordPress or another CMS for publishing. Approved posts are scheduled through the CMS API with their publish date. Nobody has to paste final copy between browser tabs again.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Decide how long a reviewer has before a reminder goes out, and when the content lead hears about a stalled draft. For design work, set the number of revision rounds in the brief and name who takes any round past it.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Run one week of real drafts through the app before the whole team moves over. Check that every draft reached the right person, that comments made it back to the writer, and that approved posts kept their dates.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Most content teams already approve work; the log shows where it waits. Each month, sort approvals by time spent in review and look at the slowest stage. Move it earlier, give it a backup, or make it conditional.
